In ancient Babylon, mathematics emerged as a practical tool for managing agriculture, trade, taxation, and astronomy. Babylonian scribes recorded calculations on clay tablets using a sophisticated base-sixty system, the ancestor of our division of hours into minutes and seconds. They developed methods for solving linear and quadratic equations, calculated areas and volumes, and used numerical tables to support commercial and administrative work. Their astronomical observations also encouraged systematic patterns, laying foundations for later mathematical science.

Ancient Egypt developed mathematics for similarly practical purposes. Egyptian scribes used a decimal system, fractions, and geometry to survey land after the annual flooding of the Nile. The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus shows procedures for multiplication, division, proportions, and calculating the areas of fields and volumes of granaries. Egyptian mathematics was largely procedural rather than theoretical, but it demonstrated how numerical reasoning could support engineering, architecture, and government.

Greek mathematics transformed calculation into deductive knowledge. During the sixth century BCE, thinkers such as Thales and Pythagoras sought universal principles behind mathematical relationships. Pythagoreans studied numerical patterns and geometry, while Euclid later organized existing knowledge in *The Elements*, a monumental work based on definitions, axioms, and proofs. Euclid’s geometry shaped mathematical education for centuries. Archimedes advanced geometry, mechanics, and approximation, estimating the value of pi and calculating areas and volumes through methods resembling integral calculus. Apollonius developed the geometry of conic sections, which later became crucial to astronomy and physics.

Mathematical progress continued beyond Greece. Indian mathematicians developed the decimal place-value system and formalized the use of zero as both a number and a positional symbol. Indian scholars also advanced algebra, trigonometry, and methods for solving equations. Their work passed into the Islamic world, where scholars translated Greek and Indian texts while creating new mathematics. In ninth-century Baghdad, Al-Khwarizmi systematized algebra, a word derived from his work’s title, and helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals. Islamic mathematicians refined trigonometric functions, studied polynomial equations, and preserved mathematical knowledge during periods when much of Europe had limited access to classical texts.

From the twelfth century onward, European scholars encountered Arabic and Greek mathematics through translation centers in Spain and Italy. Fibonacci popularized Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe through *Liber Abaci*, making commercial calculation more efficient. The Renaissance encouraged renewed interest in algebra, perspective, navigation, and scientific measurement. Mathematicians such as Cardano, Tartaglia, and Ferrari developed general solutions for cubic and quartic equations, while Viète introduced systematic symbolic notation.

By the seventeenth century, mathematics was closely connected to emerging modern science. Descartes united algebra and geometry through coordinate systems, allowing curves to be represented by equations. Fermat contributed to number theory, analytic geometry, and optimization. Building on these developments, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz independently created calculus. Their methods described continuous change, motion, curves, areas, and accumulation. Differential calculus studied rates of change, while integral calculus studied quantities gathered over intervals.
